li.a: Human Rights Watch: Ethiopia: Eritrean Forces Massacre Tigray Civilians
Human Rights Watch: Ethiopia's Axum Findings Ignore Massacre of Civilians
Al Jazeera: Killings in Axum by Eritrea troops 'may amount to war crimes'
Associated Press, published by The Spokesman-Review: Amnesty report describes Axum massacre in Ethiopia's Tigray
allAfrica: War of Words Over Massacre in Ethiopia's Holy City
Associated Press, published by Fox News: US 'gravely concerned' by Ethiopia massacre of 'many hundreds' described in Amnesty report
LBC: Eritrea soldiers killed 'many hundreds' in Axum massacre, Amnesty says

content.p: Axum is one of the most sacred towns in Ethiopia, a place of pilgrimage whose annual festival of Saint Mary falls on 30 November. In 2020 that festival was a funeral. On 28 and 29 November, during a conflict that pitted Ethiopia's federal government against the region's former ruling party, soldiers from Eritrea shot or executed several hundred of the town's residents, according to two international rights groups that interviewed survivors. Most of the dead were men and boys.

The exact number is not known. Amnesty International said "many hundreds" were killed. Human Rights Watch said it could not fix a figure, but estimated that over 200 civilians were "most likely" killed on those two days alone. A deacon who helped count bodies told the Associated Press he believed about 800 died around the city that weekend. Eritrea's government rejected the accusations, and Ethiopia's federal government denied that Eritrean soldiers were in the country at all.

Human Rights Watch dated the start of the abuses in Axum to 19 November 2020. After Tigrayan forces and militia withdrew, Ethiopian and Eritrean forces began shelling the town at about 4 p.m. and continued into the evening, according to witnesses the group interviewed. The next day, those witnesses said, soldiers fired indiscriminately at civilians, including at Saint Mary's hospital. Amnesty reached the same starting date by its own interviews and said the shelling struck the city without discrimination and that people trying to flee were fired on.

For about a week afterwards the occupying forces pillaged, Human Rights Watch reported. Residents described looted shops, a looted hospital pharmacy and a bank. A video that the group analysed appeared to show the pharmacy of Saint Mary's hospital on 30 November with drawers open and empty medicine boxes on the floor. Several residents said they saw Ethiopian soldiers join in the looting; most said the Ethiopian troops simply stood by. One resident told the group that when he asked a soldier why he did nothing, the answer was: "We need an order from above."

Residents also told Human Rights Watch that Ethiopian federal forces with heavy weapons left Axum on 26 November, heading toward Shire, and that about 50 more Eritrean soldiers arrived the next day and set up near a technical college on May Quho hill. Those who stayed behind were, in the words of one young resident, "emotional and upset" about what the soldiers were doing to the town.

Shortly after dawn on 28 November, a group of 10 to 30 Tigrayan militia filed out from behind the old Saint Mary's church toward May Quho, according to Human Rights Watch. Townspeople, mostly young men and boys, followed on impulse. Two participants said some youths seized assault rifles from an abandoned Tigrayan camp; others had only sticks, knives and stones. One participant said none of them had discussed it beforehand or been trained.

Witnesses said the youths attacked and killed about 10 Eritrean soldiers who were getting water near the hill. Gunfire followed, and Eritrean troops fired toward the town and the hill. Four congregants leaving morning prayers at Saint Mary's said the shooting sent hundreds running. A man watching from his hotel described seeing a boy of no more than 12 fall from the mountain after Eritrean snipers fired. The clashes lasted until about 4:30 p.m., when Eritrean forces called for reinforcements, who arrived firing heavy weapons from the direction of Adwa and forced the militia and youths to retreat into town.

Amnesty framed the killings as retaliation for that morning's assault by a few local militiamen and residents carrying sticks and stones. Human Rights Watch said it had also reviewed a video of the exchange of fire on the hill that matched witness accounts.
content.h2: A day and a night of killing
content.p: From about 4 p.m. on 28 November until the following morning, witnesses told Human Rights Watch, Eritrean soldiers shot residents or executed them on the streets and in house-to-house searches. Young men and boys appeared to be the targets. Amnesty's report said the soldiers shot civilians as they fled, lined men up and shot them in the back, and refused to let grieving families gather the dead.

The accounts the rights groups gathered are specific. A student told Human Rights Watch that soldiers led six neighbours outside, made them take off their belts and shoes, lined them up and fired. A teacher who opened his door to see what was happening, and cried out that he was a civilian, was shot twice, a witness said. A driver hiding on the third floor of a motel near May Quho watched soldiers lead people out, line four men against a wall and shoot them while two women pleaded. A man who had found shelter in an unfinished building told Amnesty he saw six Eritrean soldiers shoot a neighbour with a heavy machine gun mounted on a vehicle near the Mana Hotel. Another witness said soldiers shot a man and then forced a pregnant woman and two children who were with him to kneel by his body.

One man described visiting a relative whose two children had been killed in the house-to-house raids. The soldiers, he said, had locked the compound door behind them, and she was left alone with the bodies for a day and a half.

When the shooting seemed to ease, people who tried to collect the dead were fired on, several residents told Human Rights Watch. By the evening of 29 November, Eritrean forces had detained hundreds of men and boys at no fewer than three sites, the group reported. Three soldiers entered Saint Mary's church and took men who were sheltering there; one witness said around 50 were led out barefoot. At makeshift sites in open pits near the airport, detainees said, three men were shot in front of the others. That evening a soldier ordered the detainees released, with a warning that anyone who resisted further would meet the same fate as the dead.

Both organisations said survivors identified the perpetrators by the same marks. Survivors pointed to trucks with Eritrean licence plates, uniforms unlike those of the Ethiopian army, the Tigrinya dialect spoken in Eritrea, and the plastic "Congo" shoes associated with Eritrean soldiers. Amnesty's witnesses added that some soldiers had three scars on each temple, which marked them as Beni-Amir, an ethnic group found in Sudan and Eritrea but absent from Ethiopia. Some Eritrean soldiers wore the Ethiopian army uniform, but were still recognised by their shoes, witnesses said.

Human Rights Watch obtained a list of 166 names of people allegedly killed in Axum in November. Of those, 21 matched names of people that its interviewees said had been killed on 28 and 29 November. The group also described how it reached its estimate of more than 200: from interviews with elders, community members collecting identity cards of the dead, and people who helped retrieve bodies.

On 29 November, according to Amnesty's witnesses quoted by the Associated Press, Eritrean soldiers refused to let people pick up the dead, saying that the Eritreans' own dead would be buried first. The report said most burials seem to have taken place on 30 November, with more bodies found in the days after. Some wounded people died for lack of care, witnesses said, because hospitals had been looted or health workers had fled. Amnesty cited satellite images showing newly disturbed soil beside churches.

Human Rights Watch described bodies loaded onto carts and taken to churches. Some were placed in existing cement chambers at Arbatu Ensessa church, and others in mass graves, a practice at odds with Orthodox funeral rites. Over a dozen Muslims were buried at a separate site north of Saint Mary's, residents said. A day labourer said he started at 8 a.m. on 30 November and collected about 20 bodies from near the church, the bus station and the Abnet Hotel. On May Quho, one man said, hyenas had eaten corpses; he counted around 25 remains that could not be identified. "Our festival became a funeral," a mourner told the group.
Residents said journalists from Ethiopian state media recorded the churchyard to show the town was peaceful, rather than letting people mourn.
content.h2: Denial, investigation and a disputed finding
content.p: Word of an attack at Axum first spread through church media, after a Belgian group said in January 2021 that the cathedral church known as Maryam Tsiyon had been attacked, allAfrica reported. The Associated Press published its own account in the week before Amnesty. Amnesty's report followed on 26 February 2021. It said it had asked the Ethiopian government in December for permission to enter the region and received no reply.

The reactions split. Eritrea's information minister, Yemane Gebremeskel, said his country was "outraged and categorically rejects the preposterous accusations." Ethiopia's ambassador to Belgium, Hirut Zemene, called the alleged massacre a "very highly unlikely scenario." Ethiopia's ambassador to Qatar, Samia Zekaria Gutu, called the report "cooked". The government said it relied on "scanty information". At the same time the prime minister's office said it welcomed international help with investigations, and Ethiopia said the alleged incident in Axum would have to be thoroughly investigated.

The government-established Ethiopian Human Rights Commission took a different line. Its head, Daniel Bekele, said Amnesty's findings should be taken very seriously, and the commission's preliminary findings pointed to the killing of "an as yet unknown number of civilians by Eritrean soldiers" in Axum. On 27 February 2021 the United States Secretary of State, Antony Blinken, said the United States was "gravely concerned" and called for a full, independent, international investigation. Amnesty and Human Rights Watch each called for a United Nations-led inquiry.

In May 2021 Ethiopia's attorney general's office published its own findings. According to Human Rights Watch, the press release said most of those killed were fighters who had died in clashes with Eritrean troops, not civilians. Human Rights Watch replied that the release ignored the week of pillage and the 24 hours of killing that began after the clashes had ended, and that Eritrean officials were already treating the findings as vindication. It argued that an independent international inquiry might be the only route to justice for victims' families.
The opened pages report no prosecution of any soldier or commander for the killings at Axum.
